packs.title: Arlington at full scale
packs.promise: Stadium shapes, museum stories and room to breathe.

q.s: Collect a person’s story with care.
st: Enter with an Exhibit Deck ticket and choose one recipient story that you feel comfortable reading.
Collect three details from the display: the person’s name, a circumstance described in their story, and an action they took. Copy facts accurately without trying to recreate the event.
Read enough context to separate what the display states from your own interpretation. If a story feels distressing, choose another.
Write one thoughtful sentence about the person, using your three details. Keep the response about the individual rather than treating the medal as a souvenir.

q.s: Walk a short paved River Legacy segment.
st: At the main park area, locate the open paved shared-use path and identify the point you will return to.
Walk or roll toward the first path junction at a comfortable pace, up to about five minutes. Notice one change in shade and one change in sound.
Turn around at the junction or sooner if the route is closed, crowded or uncomfortable. Retrace the same open paved segment.
At your starting point, write a two-part route note: what changed on the outward leg, and what you recognized on the return. A short route counts.

q.s: Give a memorial space your attention.
st: Approach the open memorial area and quietly read a name, phrase or dedication that is actually visible.
Take three minutes in a comfortable sitting or standing place. Let yourself notice the setting without trying to make a photograph.
Write one thing the memorial asks you to remember and one detail of the surrounding park you noticed while pausing.
Leave the space as you found it. A brief, private response is enough; no declaration or conversation is required.

packs.title: Arlington, one block at a time
packs.promise: A downtown walk that reaches College Park.

st: Enter the heritage park during its public window and identify the Watson Log House, Jopling-Melear Cabin and North Side School using signs or the host.
For each building, collect one visible construction detail: a wall surface, roof shape, doorway or window. Stay in open areas.
Read one supplied date or historical marker. Pair that sourced fact with the correct building, without treating all three as the same era.
Make a three-row comparison in notes. Choose one difference that would help you recognize the buildings without their signs.

q.s: Draw a public landmark without its labels.
st: Choose an open dry place with a view of the tower and fountain form.
Reduce the landmark to five lines: one tall edge, one clock outline and three lines for its base or lion forms. You may describe the five lines in words instead.
Make a second version from a slightly different open viewpoint, or change the order of your five written lines.
Choose the version that makes the tower easiest to recognize and explain why in one sentence.

q.s: End the walk with three minutes of listening.
st: Choose a comfortable open place and put your phone away for three minutes.
During the first minute, notice a nearby sound; during the second, notice a farther sound. Silence or an absence of sound also counts.
During the third minute, let the two settle together without trying to identify every source.
Write a tiny sound score using two words and one pause mark. Add one sentence about how the end of the walk feels compared with its start.
